hypochondriacus.c: HYPOCHONDRIACUS AffeBus, Is ( faith Blanchard ) a kind of Convulsive Passion or Affedli - on, arising from the flatulent and pungent Humours in the Spleen or Sweet - bread, which afflidts the Nervous and Membranous Parts. Or, as others fay, it proceeds from Windy Hu - hours bred in the Hypochondrcs, whence a black Flegm ariseth that infedfs the Animal Spirits, and they the Mind, and is what they call Hypochondriac f Melancholy.

hypochondriumorsubcart.c: HYPOCHONDRIUM, or Subcart ilagineum, is the upper Part or Region of the Abdomen, under the Cartilages of the Chest or short Ribs: In the Right Hypochondrium lies the Liver, and a part of the Stomach; in the Left the Spleen, and a greater part of the Stomach.

hypochyma.c: HYPOCHY MA, is a depraved Sight / whereby Gnats, Cobwebs, / little Clouds, or such - like, seem to swim before the Eyes. The Cause of it seems to consist in turbid Humours, or sometimes in the Op - tick Nerves, whose little Pores are obstructed by the Matter that is thrust into them. Blanchard.

hypocratismanica.c: HYPOCRATIS Manica, Hypocrates his Sleeve: See Manica Hypocratis.

hypogastrick.c: HYPOGASTRICK - ARTERY, is by some said to be a Branch of the internal lliaca, and diftri - butes it Leis among the parts of the Hypogafirium, to the Bladder, Rectum ( in Females to the outer and inner Side of the Matrix and Vagina ) VoficuLs Se - min ales, Proftata Penis, and to the Os Sacrum, and all Parts continued in the Pelvis: Then it gives two considerable Branches, which go out of the lower Belly; the Firftpaffes under the Pyriformis, and goes to the Glutai; the Second goes to the Obturator es and the Gluteus Major.

hypogastrium.c: HYPOGASTRIUM, is the Iowermoft Region of the Abdomen, reaching from three Inches below the Navel, to the Abdomen, Os Pubis, and Groins,

hypoglossisorranula.c: HYPOGLOSSIS, or Ranula, is an Inflammation or Exulceration under the Tongue: Also a Medicine that takes away the Afperky of the Larynx, Blanchard.

hypomochlionorprop.c: HYPOMOCHLION, or Prop, in Mechanicks, ' signifies the Roller, which is usually fet under the Leaver, or under Stones or pieces of Timber, to the end that they may be more easily lifted up or removed.

hypophthalmia.c: HYPOPHTHALMIA, is a pain in the Eye un - der the Horney Tunick. Blanchard. HYPOPHORiE, are deep, gaping, and fiftuloas Ulcers. Blanchard.

hypophyllospermous.c: HYPOPHYLLOSPERMOUS - PLANTS, are such as bear their Seeds on the Backfides of their Leaves, as the Capillaries See that Word.

hypopyon.c: HYPOPYON, is a gathering of Matter under the Horney Tunick of the Eye, which sometimes covers the whole Pupil, hindering the Sight, and sometimes encompasses the Circle of the Iris, like the paring of a Nail, whence ’ tis called Onyx os Unguis.

hypospathysmus.c: HYPOSPATHYSMUS, is an Incision in the Forehead, made by three Cuts or Divisions, and where the Spatula is thrust in under the Skim Blanchard.

hyposphagma.c: HYPOSPHAGMA, is a Blood - shot from a Stroke upon the Eye.

hypostasisvrina.c: HYPOSTASIS Vrina, is that thick Substance which generally subsides at the Bottom of the U - rine.

hypostaticalprinciples.c: HYPOSTATICAL Principles; Par ace ! Jus, and his Followers, called the three Chymical ones, Salt, Sulphur, and. Mercury, lb.

hypotenar.c: HYPOTENAR, is aMufcIe which helps to draw the Little - finger from the reft. HYPOTHeNAR, is the Space from the Fore to the Little - finger. Blanchard.

hypothenuse.c: HYPOTHENUSE, in a Right - angled Triangle, is that Side which subtends the Right - angle, and consequently the longest. The Square of this Line in a Right - angled and Right - lined Triangle, is al - ways equal to the Sum of the Squares of the other two Sides, Prop.. e.. Euclid: See the Demon - station under Triangle.

hypothesis.c: HYPOTHESIS, the fame with Supposition ? When for the Solution of any Phenomena in Natu - ral Philosophy, Astronomy, &c. some Principles are supposed as granted, that from thence an intelligible and plausible Account of the Causes, the Effects of the proposed Phenomena may be given, the laying down or supposing such Principles to be granted, is called an Hypothesis; and the thing said to be ac - countable easily according to that Hypothesis, if it give a clear and easy Solution of the Phenomena. Wherefore an Hypothesis is a Supposition of that which is not, for that which may be; and it matters not whether what is supposed be true or not, but it must be poflibie, and should always be pro - table. An Hypothesis, in some Sense, falls in with a Sy - stem: But this Word is usually taken in rested to the Univerle, and in Relation to the Difpofidons of the Heavens, aud the Motion of the Stars: An ela - borately contrived Hypothesis about which, is called a Syfiem; as the Ptolemaic ! Copernican, or Tycho - nian Syfiem.

hypotrachelioninarchitecture.c: HYPOTRACHELION, in Architecture, is the Top or Neck of a Pillar, or the most fender part of it which toucheth the Capital, U It is taken by some for that part of the Tuscan and Dorick, Capitals which lies between the Echi - nus and the Afiragal and is otherwise called the Cottar, Gorge, or Fri c of the Chapter.

hypotyposis.c: HYPOTYPOSIS, is a lively and ead Descrip - tion of any Object made in Fancy.

hypozoma.c: HYPOZOMA, is a Membrane that parts two Cavities, as the Mediofiinumin the Thorax. Blan - chard.

hysteralgia.c: HYSTERALGIA, is a pain in the Womb, pro - ceeding from an Inflammation, or otherwise. Blan - chard.,

hysterica.c: HYSTERICA, are Medicines against the Dis - cafesof the Womb.

HYSTERICA - PASSIO, Fits of the Mother, is ( according to some ) a Convulsion of the Nerves of the Par Vagum, and Intercostal in the Abdomen, pro - ceeding from a pricking Irritation or Explosion of the Spirits: This Distemper does not always, nor indeed usually, depend upon the Womb, as is com - monly thought: ’ Tis seen sometimes in Men, be - cause the Spleen, Pancreas, and other adjacent Bowels, are often the Cause of it. Blanchard. Dr. Purcell, in his Book of Vapours, attempts to prove, and with probability, That the Cause of Hy - strick Fits is neither the fix Non - natural Things, nor the solid parts of the Body, nor the Blood, nor a - tiydf the Recrements, nor the Womb, nor Vapours thence arising nor the irregular disorderly Motion of the Animal Spirits; nor is it in the Chyle, or iri the Ferment of the Stomach or Guts, &c. But he supposes the true Cause to be Crudities and Indige - ftions in the Aliments, which, by little and little,, gather together in the Wrinkles and Folds of the Stomach and Guts; where they ( as he supposes ) lie for some time without much sensible Motion or Fermentation within themselves, till at last, by the Heat of the Circumjacent Parts, their grosser Says are divided and put into Motion j which Ferment - tion is augmented by the various Juices which flow into the Guts from the many Glands which are pla - ced in the Lower Belly; and by this means they " are so dissolved and liquified, as to enter in by the Hence LaBre into the Blood, where they produce those Accidents which cause the Symptoms of this various Disease.

hysteromotocia.c: HYSTEROMOTOCIA, or SeBio Gafdrea, is a cutting the Child out of the Womb; which is done thus: You make a Semi - ltinar SeBion under the Navel along the Linen Alba, the Cavity whereof looks towards the said Line; then according to the leading of the Fibres, the Foetus being extracted after the Section, the Wound in the Womb con - trails of it self, so that the Blood scarce flows more plentifully than in a Natural Birth; but if the Mo - ther be Dead, choose the most convenient place you can. Blanchard.

hysterotomia.c: HYSTEROTOMIA, is an Anatomical DifledH - on of the Womb. I C E

hole.c: HOLE, in the Sea phrase, is the fame as hallow: They fay, ’ tis good floating, when as a Ship fails towards the hoar, fine finds by her sounding, it grows hallow by degrees, and not too, suddenly; for then a Snip may go in safety.

HOLE - D, was the Tuesday Fortnight after Eajler - Day; and was anciently celebrated with Sports and Rejoycings, in Memory of many of the Danes being kill ’ d on that Day, and the reft expel ’ d the Kingdom. This was done A. D.. in the Reign of K. Ethelred.

habenteshomines.c: HABENTES Homines, Sailing - Men; as they are call ’ d in, a Charter of Cenulph King of the Mercians, Anno zi. Du Frefne will have these to be no more than Divides, Rich Men: But no doubt the Word implies a ftridter Sence and signified either the King ’ s Guard or Retinue, which were at the King ’ s Pleasure to be Feasting - Men, or plentifully enter - tained at the Houses of his Tenants: Or rather, those Old Servants which were commended to the Religious by the King; and so fafined on them for Corrodies, or Maintenance for Life, Some think that they were only Pledges and Sureties, or Friburghs; which under their Chief or Princi - pal Ty thing Man, were to keep the King ’ s Peace, and to be accountable for the Breach of it.

habitation.c: HABITATION, in the Civil Law, is the Term for one of the Personal Services, by which a Man hath a Right to live in the House of ano - ther without Prejudice to the Propriety

haybote.c: HAYBOTE, was a Recompence made for the Violation of Holy Orders, or Violence offer ’ d to Persons in them,

hail.c: HAIL. Dr. Wallis in a Letter from Oxon to the Secretary of the Royal Society, and Printed in the TranJdBions, observes that Hail is very often an Attendant on Thunder and Lightning; ( of which, fee Thunder in this Volume. ) And ’ tis well known, that in our artificial Congelati - ons, a Mixture of Snow and Nitre, or even com - mon Salt, will cause a. very sudden Congelation of Water. Now the fame in the Clouds may cause Hail - Stones and the rather, because not only in some prodigiously great, but also in common Hail - Stones there seems somewhat like Snow ra - ther than Ice, in the midst of them. And as to those very large Hail - Stones, weighing or of a Pound; by the violence of their Fall ’ tis mani - sest they muff have descended from a great Height: And tho ’ perhaps in their first Concretion, or Congelation, their Bulk might be but of the moderate Size of common Hail, yet in their long Descent, if the Medium, through which they fell, were alike inclined to Congelation, they might receive a great Accession to their Bulk, by, per - haps, many of them coalescing and incorporating into one; as in that strange Shower of Hail in December i jz. whereof there hung on the Trees a great deal in the form of Icicles, of a Foot or more in length.

hailorkfolk.c: HAIL ORKFOLK; i. e. Holy Work - folk, or People who hold Lands for the Service of Re - pairing or Defending fame Church or Sepulchre:. For which pious Labours they were excuse for - merly from Feudal and Military Services.

hawse.c: HAWSE, is an oid Gothic Word, signifying a Society of Merchants combine ’ d together for the good Usage and safe Passage of Merchant - die from Kingdom to Kingdom. This Society was, and in part is yet, endow ’ d with many large Privileges of Princes respectively within their Territories. heatgreatbodies.c: HEAT, Great Bodies are capable of prefer - ving Heat for a long while; their Parts mutual - ly increasing one anothers Heat. And it may be; that a very great dense and fix ’ d Body, when heated beyond such a degree, may emit Light so copiously, that by such Emiilion, and by the Re - action of its Light, and by the Reflexions and Refraction of the R ys within its hidden Meatus, it may come to grow still hotter and hotter, as deriving more Degrees of Heat by thole ways, than it can of Cold by any other: And by this means itmay come to attain a Heat, like that of the Sun: For the Sun and the fix ’ d Stars seem only vast Globes of Earth vehemently heated; and whose Heat is preserved by their great Magni - tude, and by the mutual A & ion and Re - adion that there is between them and the Light which they emit. And their Parts are preserved from evapora - ting in Flame and Fume; not only by the great Fixity of their Nature; bur also by the mighty Weight and Density of the Atmolphere which environ them, which press them every way with a great Nifuf, and condense their Vapours - and Exhalations, when ever they are emitted. For we fee that Water, but moderately heated, will boil with violence when the Pressure of our Atmosphere is taken off in the Exhausted Recei - ver. And a Mixture of Tin and Lead, being plac ’ d on a red - hot Iron in vacuo, will emit copious Fumes, and even some Flame, which yet in our Air will scarce visibly smoke. Vid. Qu.. New - ton. Opt. p.. Edit. Lar. Heat conduces very much to the Fluidity of Bodies, by lessening the Tenacity of their Parrs; for ir renders many Bodies fluid, which other - wife are not so; and increases the Fluidity of Tenacious Liquors, as of Oyl, Ballam, Ho - new, &c. and by the fame reason lessens their Refilling Force: And yet it doth not much lessen the Refilling Force of Water; which it muff do, if that Force arise chiefly from the Attrition or Tenacity of its Parts; and consequently it doth, not arise from thence, but from the Vis Inertht V Materice.

helisphericalline.c: HELISPHERICAL Line, is the Rhumb Line in Navigation; and is so call ’ d because on the Globe it winds round the Pole spirally, and still comes nearer and nearer to it, but can ’ t terminate in it.

The Ovens wherein the Lapis Gala - minaris, or Calamine, is baked, have ? a Hearth made on one side of the Oven, divided from the Oven it less by a Partition open at the Top. by which the Flame pastes over, and so heats and Vol. II. Besides these there are Six others, which are properly called Heralds, according to their Ori - ginals, as they were Created to attend Dukes, & e. in their Martial Expeditions; as York Lan - casier, Somerset, Richmond, Chejler, and Windforl There also are four others call ’ d Marjhals, or Purfuivants at Arms, reckon ’ d after a manner in the Number of Heralds, and do commonly sue - led in the Place of Herald when they die, &c and these are call ’ d Blue - Mantle, Rouge Cross, Rouge Dragon, and Port - Cullis.

herbengerorharbinger.c: HERBENGER, or Harbinger, is an Officer in the King or Queen ’ s House, who alotteth the Noblemen and those of the Houfhold their Lodgings. HERETICO Comburendo: See Herctico, &c l

heriot.c: HERIOT, was originally a Proportion of Horse and Armotir according to the Quality of the Deceas ’ d: This was settled by the Laws of K. Canutus, cap.. and is still ( usually ) the belt Riding Horse of which a Tenant dies possess ’ d.

HERIOT CuRom, was when a Tenant for Life was by Custom oblige ’ d to such a payment at his Death; which Payment to be made not only by the next Heir in Blood, but by any the next SuccefTor. In Abbeys of Royal Patronage, at the Death or Cession of the Abbot, his Cup and Horse were paid as an Heriot to the King: Those also who held in Bondage and Villenage paid Hericts. The Religious Appropriators re - serve ’ d the Live Heriot s ( /. c. such as were paid in Cattle ) to themselves, and allow ’ d the inanimate ones of small value to the Vicar: And feme Ap - propriators. had a Heriot from the Vicar when he died. heriotservice.c: HERIOT Service was a Reserve by Charter or other Conveyance, and made one Condition of the Tenure of Estates in Fee Simple; which is now for the most part extinguish ’ d.

hermitage.c: HERMITAGE, stri & ly signified a Convent of Hermits or Friars Minors, who, under the Infti - tuition and Discipline of St. Paul, inhabited Be - sorts and solitary places. But this name at last came to be attributed to any one Religious Cell, built and endow ’ d in some private and recluse place, and then annex ’ d to some larger Abbey, of which the Prelate or Governour was called Hermita. Dr. Rennet's Glossary. HERMIT AN, is the Name of a dry North and North - Easterly " Wind, usually, which blows on the Coast of Guinea in Africki but some times it blows alio from other Points.

hermitorium.c: HERMITORIUM, is the Oratory or Chapel belonging to an Hermitage.

( See the Fig. in Homodromw. ) The Dung - fork and Prong are Leavers of this kind, whose Hypomochlion is usually the Knee of the Workman: And all Pincers, Sheers, Scif - fars, Cutting - Knives faftrfed to Blocks are double.

hayboteorhaybote.c: HAYBOTE, or Haybote, was anciently the Saxon Term lor the Liberty granted to a Tenant sot Cutting so much Under - wood, Bullies, (. as was necessary for Mending and Maintaining the Hedges or Fences belonging ro his Land.

hidage.c: HID AGE, was a Royal Aid or Tribute rais ’ d in such a Proportion on every Hide of Land. William the Conqueror imposed Six Shillings on every Hide; and William Rufus Four Shillings; and K. Henry I. Three Shillings. When the Lord paid Hidage to the King, the Tenants paid a Proportion to the Lord of the Mannor. King Ethelred, when the Danes landed at Sand - wich, rais ’ d this Hidage so, that every o Hides of Land found an Arm ’ d Ship; and every Hides found a Jack and a Saddle.

hideofland.c: HIDE of Land, or Plough - Land, was as much as one Plow could Cultivate in a Year; for the Quantity was never exprelly determin ’ d: Some call it, some, and some Acres. One Hide of Land at Chejlerton in the th ol Hen. II. contain'd Acres: And in the th of Hen. III. the yearly Value of a Hide of Land at Blechef - don in Oxfordfhire was Forty Shillings. KJnnet's Paroch. Antiq, Bede calls it Familiam, implying by it, that it was as much as wou ’ d maintain a Family. The Distribution of England by Hides of Land is very ancient: Mention being made of it in the Laws of King Ina, cap.. And Henry I. to Marry his Daughter, had Three Shillings from H o M every Hide of Land. This Tax was call ’ d Hi - age: See Hidage.

hip.c: HIP - Roof in Architecture, is such a Roof as hath neither Gable - Heads, S bread - Heads, nor Jerkin - Heads: ( By which is meant such Heads as are both Gable and Hip at the fame End; that is. Gable as far as the Cott or Beam, and then their over short Hips which shut up with their Tops to the Tops of a pair of Rafters, call ’ d Singlers by the Country Workmen. ) For a Hip - Roof hath Rafters as long, and with the Angles at the Foot, ( c. at the Ends of Buildings, as it hath on the Sides: And the Feet of the Rafters on the Ends of such Buildings as have Hip - Roofs, ( land on the fame Plane, vi. parallel to the Horizon, and at the fame Height from the Foundation with the Rafters at the Sides of the Roofs. These Hip - Roofs some call Italian Roofs.

hipsinarchitecture.c: HIPS, in Architecture, are those Pieces of Timber which are at the Corners of a Roof: They are a good deal longer than the Rafters, because of their oblique Position; for they are level at every Angle. The Country Workmen call them Corners; and by some they are call ’ d Principal Rafters, by others Sleepers. As Rafters have four plain Sides, these have usually five,

hobelers.c: HOBELERS, were formerly a fort of Light - Horse - Men, which rode on small nimble Horses, and with only light Armour on so that - they were fit ( like our Dragoons ) for any expeditious Service: At length they became ty ’ d by their Tenure, to maintain a little light Nag; for giv - ing expeditious Notice of any Invasion or Dan - ger: See Ed.. c.. Ed.. c.,, and Cambd. Britan.

hobits.c: HOBITS, are a fort of small Mortars from to Inches Diameter: Their Carriages are like those of Guns, only much shorter; They are very good for Annoying the Enemy at a distance with small Bombs, which they will throw two or three Miles: Or in keeping of a Pass, being loaded with Cartouches.

horometricalmethod.c: HOROMETRICAL Method of finding the Longitude atSea, is that of the Computation of the Measure of the Way of a Ship bet. place andplace; i. e. of observing the several Rhumbs or Lines in which the Ship faileth; and whit Way she hath made, or how many Leagues and parts of a League fine hath run.

hogenhine.c: HOGENHINE, was formerly the Term for one that coming Guest - wife to an Inn or House, lay there the third Night: After which he was accounted one of the Family; and the Host was answerable for his Breach of the King ’ s Peace. In the Laws of K. Edward, fet forth by Lambert, he is call ’ d Agenhinc; and often in other places Third - Night Awnehinc.

holetuesday.c: HOLE Tuesday - Money, was a Duty paid by the Tenants to their Landlord, to have leave to celebrate the Hose - Day.

homagiumreddere.c: HOMAGIUM Reddere, was renouncing Ho - mage, when a Vassal made a solemn Declara - tion of disowning and defying his Lord; for which there was a fet Form and Method pre - scribe ’ d by the Feudatory Laws, HOMO - HIS

Here the Weight moves the fame way with the Power: Whence this kind of VeBis takes its Name of Homodr omus. Whereas, in the other Leaver, the Weight N is raised up by means of the Obex or Hypomoclion H; while the Power at A, the other End of the Lea - ver, descends; and therefore this is called Here - rodromus. Of this Homodromus kind of Leavers, are the Rudders and Oars of Ships and Boats; as also their Mails,

honor.c: HONOR, is used for the noble fort of Seig - niories, whereon other Inferior Lordfhips and Manners do depend, by performance of Customs and Services to those that are Lords over them: And it seems as if none were Honors originally, but such as belong ’ d to the King, tho given af - terwards in Fee to Noblemen,, The Manner of Creating these Honors may in part be collected from the Statutes H.. c.. where Hampton - Court is made an Honor: And H.. c.,. where Grafton and Amp thill are made Honors. There are many other Honors in England; fee H.. c., &c.
HONOR - Courts, are such Courts as are held within the above - mention ’ d Honors.

honoraryservices.c: HONORARY Services, are such as are inch - dent to Grand Sergeantry, and annexed usually to some Honor.

hook.c: HOOK - PAzj, are taper Iron Pins, with an hook Head; and are used to pin the Frame of a Floor or Roof together, by being put in through - the Pin - holes in the Morteffes and Tendons, whilst it is framing or fitting into its due Position: As soon as which is done, these Hook P ins are struck out, and ’ tis pinn ’ d up fall with Wpoden Piss.

horizontal.c: HORIZONTAL - L / e in Dialling, is a Line drawn on any Plane parallel to the Horizon. It is drawn on an EreCt or Reclining Plane by a Level; or by applying a Quadrant to the Edge of a Ruler so, as that the String and Plummet Shall cut. or Degreees in the Limb.

hospitallers.c: HOSPITALLERS, were the Knights of a Religious Order; so called, because they builded an Hospital at Jerufalcm, wherein Pilgrims were received. To these, when the Tern piers were suppress ’ d by the Council of Vienne in France, P. Clement transferr ’ d that Order. Their chief Abode is now ax Malta, and they are call ’ d Knights I of Malta. All the Lands and Goods of such as were here in England were given to the Crown s See H.. c..

housebote.c: HOUSEBOTE, the fame with Ejlovers, or an Allowance of necessary Timber out of the Lord ’ s Wood, for the Repair and Support of a House or Tenement.

howkerorhoucre.c: HOWKER, or Houcre, is a Vessel much used by the Dutch; built something like a Pink, but Masted and Ring d like a Hoy. They carry from to Tun: And with a small number of Hands will go to the Eajl - Indies They Tack soon and ( hort; will Sail well, and lie near the Wind; and will live almost in any Sea.

hulks.c: HULKS, are large Vessels, having their Gun - Decks from to Foot long, and from to Foot broad. They will carry from to Tons. But their chiefeft Use is for let - ting in Mails into Ships, and the like. Though anciently the Word Hull a seems to signifie a small Vessel.

hundred.c: HUNDRED, is a Part of a Shire or County, properly so called, because it contained Ten De - cennx or Tythings; And either because at first there were an Hundred Families in each Hun - dred; or else that the Hundred found a hundred Men for the King ’ s Wars. These Hundred were were first Ordain ’ d by King Alfred, the th King of the West Saxons and he took the way of doing it from Germany; where Centa, or Cen - tena is a Jurifdidlion over an hundred Towns. Hence you see the Original of Hundreds, which still keep the name, and remain, in some fort, the fame, as to their Service in several re - fpedls: But their JurifdiBion is transferr ’ d to the County - Court; some few excepted, which have been by Privilege annex ’ d to the Crown, or granted to some Great Subject, and so remain still in the nature of a Franchize: And this hath been ever since the Statute of Ed... c. ?: whereby these Hundred - Courts, formerly Farm ’ d out by the Sheriffs to other Men, were reduce ’ d all, or molt of them, to the County - Court - and so remain at present. Where - ever therefore we meet with the Word Hundred - Court now, it, signifies some Franchize, where the Sheriff does j not intermeddle by his ordinary Authority, unless when they of the Hundred refuse to do their Duty.

hundredcourts.c: HUNDRED Courts, were held anciently by the Hundredarius, or Chief - Constable, of every Hundred, for better supports his Office. These Courts were held in some places once in three Weeks, and in others once a Month. And by Star. Ed.. these Hundred - Courts were reduce ’ d to the County - Courts; tho ’ in some few Hun - dreds the Old Franchises are still remaining.

hundreders.c: HUNDREDERS, are Men Empannelled, or fit to be Empanelled, on a Jury, upon a Contro - verfiej and who dwell in the Hundred where the Land in question lies. But

hundredariusthehundreder.c: HUNDREDARIUS, the Hundreder, is he that hath the Jurifdi & ion of a Hundred, and who holdeth the Hundred - Court. And sometimes ’ tis used for the Baily of the Hundred.

hundredse.c: HUNDRED Se a, was the Payment of per - synal Attendance, ordering Suit and Service at the Hundred - Court.

hundredusaffirmatus.c: HUNDREDUS Affirmatus, was the Profits of an Hundred Court, Firmed or Farmed out for a Standing Rent.
